title: EXCLUSIVE: Mellerio's Latest High Jewelry Design Takes Tips From the 1950s
text:
French jeweler Mellerio is launching gem-set gold nail ornaments, a design it patented in 1951, during the high jewelry Paris Couture Week showcases.
Forget the two-year cycle that takes a Place Vendôme cornerstone from gouaché sketch to glittering showcase. Mellerio’s latestUnveiled on Monday at the 314-year-old family-owned jeweler, three series of nail ornaments in 18-karat gold set with gems bring to life a design first patented in 1951.
It featured a frame that follows the contour of the nails, with a mesh-like design that is perforated with diamonds. For decades the initial version remained a precious curio on display in its Rue de la Paix archival showcase — and a point of fascination for artistic director Laure-Isabelle Mellerio. But don’t go calling them fake nails.
“They’re not fake, it’s real gold and real diamonds,” she joked. “They were described as decorative nail trim. ” Only two major differences exist between the 1951 version and its 2026 descendant. The first was an easy change: Mellerio reached for gold, white or yellow depending on the gem pairing, over the palladium used in the initial version.
“The real challenge was making sure this gold nail stays securely on the natural one but also making sure they could be removed easily,” the artistic director said. To that end, the team imagined a system based on suction cups instead of the original rubberized seals.
This elegantly simple solution unlocked a project she’d “wanted to do for a long time” and felt aligned with a boom time for nail art and embellished manicures, sometimes with precious and even sculpted elements.
“It has really become a new territory of expression so it felt of the moment to revisit our ornaments,” she said. Five shapes and several sizes were made, to accommodate different nail beds. No obligation to buy a full hand, either. Mellerio is adamant that the true charm lies in composition and play, so nails are sold individually.
“The idea is that the wearer can compose their set each day, depending on their mood and events,” she said. “It’s always about this freedom that is important to us in the spirit of our jewels. ” Priced at 5,000 euros per ornament, three colorways have been unveiled. One reprises the all-white aesthetic of its forebear in white gold and matching diamonds, a second set plays on black diamonds, and the last one comes in yellow gold with multicolored gemstones.
While little information exists on the context in which these were initially developed — only the patent remains in the archives — Mellerio feels that is an affiliation to the world of fashion and couture.
“The 1950s were very much a time for accessories, with all those little bags and eyewear that were made,” she said. The new designs also reinforce the house’s current throughline of “joaillerie décomplexée,” which loosely translates as “effortless jewelry. ” “It’s very contemporary but it connects us to our history because were invented 80 years ago,” she said.
“That’s also something I’m very attached to: ensuring that the current creations of the house are rooted in patrimony. ”There’s a richly ornamental design redolent of Renaissance pieces that will draw on colored gems and enamel worked in gradients, and a long adjustable black-and-white sautoir number that takes an Art Deco approach to trellises, with a combination of vine-like branches interspersed with onyx and pearls.
The third piece continues the Talisman line, introducing tantalum in Mellerio’s creative vocabulary for “an object that came from space. ” Both the pendant and the chain were crafted from the metal, a feat that called for Swiss watchmaking expertise, with a partner “who was working for a jewelry house for the first time,” Mellerio said.
“It was fascinating and I even imagined smaller medals that we are going to launch,” she continued. “That echoes the innovation that we must be in today. ” These designs also come as a new chapter is opening for the brand, which revealed on Wednesday the arrival of Amalia Cortesi as deputy chief executive officer. She succeeds Christophe Mélard, who exited in January following five years that saw the jeweler reposition itself and make inroads on the American market.
